topic: Why you forget why you walked into a room
title: Why You Forget Why You Walked In
hook_promise: Why do you forget your purpose the moment you walk into another room?

beats.narration: Why are you standing here? You walked in with a purpose. Now it's gone.
beats.visual_intent: Lead stands blank in the middle of a sunlit living room with an empty open hand, the purpose visibly gone.

shot.image_prompt: Medium shot of the lead standing in the middle of a warm sunlit living room, head tilted, eyebrows slightly raised in puzzled confusion, one mitten hand open and empty at chest height. Golden late-afternoon light with dappled shadows on the floor, a green door and a doorway visible behind.
pose_variants: Lead with both hands raised in a small shrug, brows lifted, mouth soft

beats.narration: Blame the doorway. Psychologist Gabriel Radvansky says it acts like an event boundary.
beats.visual_intent: Friend points at the doorway frame, which is painted like a glowing line dividing two spaces, while lead looks on.

shot.image_prompt: Wide shot of a warm living room, lead and friend standing side by side near a wooden doorway frame with a soft golden glow along its threshold. Friend in the teal scarf points at the doorway, lead looks at it curiously. Late afternoon sun slanting across the floor.

beats.narration: Your mind files activity into episodes, like chapters.
beats.visual_intent: Top-down view of a notebook with separate tabbed chapters, each page holding a small painted scene of a day's activity.

shot.image_prompt: Top-down insert of an open notebook on a wooden table, with colorful tabbed dividers separating several pages, each page showing a tiny painted sketch of an everyday scene. A green coffee cup sits at the corner. Warm golden light with soft shadows.

beats.narration: A new chapter starts. Your purpose stays in the old one.
beats.visual_intent: Lead stands blank in the kitchen while through the doorway behind, the living room holds a glowing sticky note left behind.

shot.image_prompt: Medium shot of the lead standing in a sunlit kitchen, looking blankly ahead, a wooden doorway behind showing the living room in the distance where a small glowing sticky note rests on a table. Golden light, plants on the counter.

beats.narration: At Notre Dame, people forgot more after a doorway than crossing the same distance in one room.
beats.visual_intent: Contrast: friend relaxed holding a note, lead blank with empty hands, to show doorway versus same-room forgetting.

shot.image_prompt: Medium shot in a warm kitchen: friend in a teal scarf stands calmly holding a small paper note, lead stands beside with empty hands and a puzzled face. A wooden doorway frame stands in the background. Golden sunlight and dappled shadows.

beats.narration: Even a virtual doorway did it, in younger and older adults.
beats.visual_intent: Lead and friend on the sofa look at a laptop showing a painted doorway, showing the effect holds on screen and across ages.

shot.image_prompt: Medium shot of lead and friend sitting on a cozy sofa in a sunlit living room, a laptop open on lead's lap showing a small painted doorway on its screen. Friend in a teal scarf points at the screen, lead leans in with interest. Warm golden light.
pose_variants: Lead leaning back with a gentle smile, eyes on the laptop screen

beats.narration: But here's the catch. Later studies found no clear effect.
beats.visual_intent: At the kitchen table, friend shakes head over a stack of study papers while lead looks doubtful.

shot.image_prompt: Close shot of lead and friend sitting at a round wooden kitchen table with a stack of papers between them and green coffee cups. Lead raises one brow, doubtful, friend in a teal scarf looks at the papers. Warm golden afternoon light.
pose_variants: Friend with head tilted, hands open in a small shrug

beats.narration: One 2021 replication saw it only when memory was already overloaded.
beats.visual_intent: Lead at the table surrounded by an overflowing stack of sticky notes and a brimming cup, showing a loaded memory.

shot.image_prompt: Close shot of the lead seated at a wooden kitchen table piled with a tall, wobbly stack of sticky notes and a brimming green coffee cup, lead looking weary with eyes drooping slightly. Warm light through the kitchen window.

beats.narration: So you forget because your mind filed the plan in the last room, especially when it's already busy.
beats.visual_intent: Lead stands in the kitchen with a hand on forehead while the glowing note sits far behind in the living room.

shot.image_prompt: Medium shot of the lead standing in a sunlit kitchen with one mitten hand on forehead, eyes closed in a small rueful smile. Through the doorway behind, a glowing sticky note rests on a living room table. Warm golden light.

beats.narration: Next time you stand there blank, blame the doorway.
beats.visual_intent: Back in the living room, lead shrugs with a laugh while friend nods knowingly, looping to the opening scene.

shot.image_prompt: Medium shot of lead and friend standing in the sunlit living room by the doorway. Lead shrugs with a warm smile, friend in a teal scarf nods and gestures kindly at the doorway. Golden light and dappled shadows.
pose_variants: Lead laughing softly with a hand on forehead

sources.claim: Psychologist Gabriel Radvansky of the University of Notre Dame says passing through a doorway acts as an "event boundary" in the mind, which separates episodes of activity and files them away.
sources.title: Walking through doorways causes forgetting, new research shows
sources.quote: “Entering or exiting through a doorway serves as an ‘event boundary’ in the mind, which separates episodes of activity and files them away,” Radvansky...

sources.claim: Researchers explain it in three parts: memories are divided into episodes, earlier episodes are harder to recall, and walking through a doorway creates a new episode, so your purpose stays stored in the previous one.
